chunks: "A MOSFET gate is basically a capacitor with an extremely high DC resistance. If nothing is driving it, it just sits wherever leakage, noise or stored charge put it.

And there are plenty of times when nothing is driving it: the microcontroller is in reset, it's booting, the pin is configured as an input, or it's powered down with the supply on the load still present.
If that floating gate drifts up toward the threshold voltage, the FET starts to conduct partway.
With a motor or solenoid on the other side, that means it can twitch or fire at power-up.
Worse, a half-on FET drops a good part of the supply voltage while carrying current, so it can get very hot very quickly. With 12 volts and a 24 ohm load, if the FET lets 0.
2 amps through, it's dropping over 7 volts, about 1. 4 watts, in a small package.
A pulldown resistor from gate to source gives the gate a defined path to ground, so whenever the pin isn't driving, the gate discharges to zero and the FET stays off.
I'd use something between 10 and 100 kilohms.
Small enough to beat leakage and noise and discharge the gate in a reasonable time, large enough that the GPIO can still drive the gate high without wasting current: 3.
3 volts across 100 k is only 33 microamps."
